paragraphs.text: In the last video, we followed one template through lit HTML. At almost every step, the hard work was done by the browser: parsing, copying, walking the DOM.

That's a big part of why lit HTML is small: about three kilobytes, compressed. All of Lit, with its component base class, is about six. This video is a tour of the platform features underneath it, and what each one does for Lit.

It starts in JavaScript. When the engine parses a tagged template literal, it has already split the fixed strings from the expressions. And the language spec makes a promise about those strings: each template literal in your code gets exactly one strings array. It's created once, it's frozen, and the same array is passed every time that literal runs.
That array is lit HTML's cache key, for free. It's also why Lit doesn't need a build step: the engine has already separated what never changes from what does.

The array has one more feature: a raw property, with the strings exactly as written. Before lit HTML treats the strings as trusted HTML, it checks that raw is there. An object that came from JSON can't have it, so data can't pose as a template.

And values are never parsed as HTML. Text goes into text nodes, and attributes go through set attribute. So a user's string can't turn into markup, unless you ask for that on purpose, with unsafe HTML.

Next, HTML. lit HTML doesn't parse HTML itself. It builds one string, and sets it as a template element's inner HTML. The browser's parser is native code, it's fast, and it follows the spec exactly, including all the irregular ways real pages write HTML.
What comes out is inert. A template's contents belong to a separate document, with no browsing context. So scripts don't run, images don't load, and custom elements don't upgrade.

And those question mark markers? For years, the parser turned anything starting with angle bracket, question mark, into a comment. But this year, HTML gained real processing instructions, as part of streaming content into place. Now, in the spec and in Chrome, angle bracket, question mark, marker, becomes a processing instruction node.

lit HTML's markers still come out as comments. A processing instruction's name can only use letters, digits, hyphens and underscores. When the parser meets the first dollar sign, the name is invalid, and the spec says to turn what it has read into a comment, starting with the question mark. That's exactly the comment lit HTML looks for.
To stamp out a template, lit HTML calls import node on its contents, with deep set to true. That's the DOM's own copy operation. Nothing is parsed again, and the copies belong to the page's document.

To find its places in the copy, it uses a tree walker. There's just one, created when lit HTML loads, with a filter that shows only elements and comments. That filter is a bit mask: one bit for elements, and the bit worth one hundred and twenty eight, for comments. The walker skips every text node in native code.

And comments make good anchors. They can sit anywhere content can, the parser keeps them, and they never render. A child part's content lives right after its comment, and new nodes go in with insert before.

Event bindings use a feature of add event listener that's easy to miss. The listener doesn't have to be a function. It can be any object with a handle event method. lit HTML's event part registers itself, and calls whichever function it holds right now. So a new arrow function on every render never touches the listener list.
The same call takes an options argument, and lit HTML passes your listener there too. So you can set capture, once, or passive as properties of the listener, right in the template.
So far, that's all lit HTML. Lit adds components, and those are the platform too.

Custom elements. Define a class for a tag name, and the browser calls it back when an element is created, connected, or when an attribute it watches changes. Lit's reactive element turns those callbacks into reactive properties.

Shadow DOM. Each element renders into its own shadow root, so its internal DOM and its styles are scoped to it, with slots for the children you pass in. There's no class name rewriting, and no global stylesheet to manage.

Constructable stylesheets. Styles written with Lit's css tag become one CSS style sheet object, shared by every instance, through adopted style sheets. A thousand instances, one parsed stylesheet. And a css literal with no expressions in it caches its sheet with the same trick as html: the strings array is the key.
Last, timing. Set three properties on a Lit element, one after another, and it renders once.

Each change calls request update, which records the change, and if no update is pending, starts one. That update begins by awaiting a promise, which lets the rest of your code run first. Then it renders once, with all three changes.

Code after an await runs in a microtask, which runs before the browser gets a chance to paint. So nobody ever sees a half-updated element. And update complete is that same promise, so your tests can await it.
So here's what the browser does for Lit.

JavaScript's tagged templates split static from dynamic, and hand over a cache key. The HTML parser and the template element turn strings into inert DOM. Import node and the tree walker copy it and find the holes. Comments hold places. Listener objects make swapping handlers cheap. Custom elements, shadow DOM and adopted style sheets give you components with scoped styles. And microtasks batch the updates.
Much of Lit's own code is the glue between these features. That's why it's small, and why so much of its speed is native code that's already in your browser.
To watch this happen to your own templates, try the lit HTML explorer. Links to the specs and the source are on the page with this video.
